about.title: I understand the system before I design the screen.
about.paragraph1: I studied Software Engineering at Universidad APEC and ended up specializing in product design. That background changed how I design: a screen is never just a screen — it’s also a set of states, rules, dependencies, and edge cases that someone will have to build and maintain.
about.paragraph2: I don’t follow a rigid process. I start by understanding how the real process works and where the friction is; sometimes that means observing, sometimes running the system myself, and sometimes I only understand the problem once I’m prototyping. I value standards, but every product needs its own way of relating to the people who use it.

about.principle3.title: Design and engineering, one conversation
about.principle3.body: The best decisions account for people and for the technical reality of the product at the same time.

meta.baseball.title: Baseball Scoreboard — Case study | Gregory Durán
case.baseball.hero.eyebrow: Case study · Product in real use
case.baseball.hero.subtitle: How I turned a scoreboard that a volunteer updated by hand — live, in front of everyone — into a console built for working under pressure and a public screen that updates itself, with no internet.
case.baseball.hero.imageAlt: Public projection screen next to the operator console during a game
case.baseball.overview.heading: The project in 30 seconds
case.baseball.ov.product: Live scoring console + public projection screen for Bible Baseball tournaments.
case.baseball.ov.context: An annual community tournament run by Ministerio Cristiano HOME, operated by volunteers at a field without reliable internet.
case.baseball.ov.problem: A single volunteer logged every play by hand on whiteboards and PowerPoint while the game kept going; any mistake was projected in front of everyone.
case.baseball.ov.role: Product Designer and front-end developer, end to end: research, interaction and UI design, prototyping, code, and iteration after real use. A personal project, built together with the organizers.
case.baseball.ov.platform: Web app: console + projection on a second screen
case.baseball.ov.status: Used in a real tournament; still evolving
case.toc.label: Case study sections
case.baseball.context.heading: I was the scoreboard operator
case.baseball.context.p1: Every year, Ministerio Cristiano HOME runs a community Bible Baseball tournament. For several editions, the score was kept on physical whiteboards and PowerPoint slides, updated by hand by a volunteer.
case.baseball.context.p2: That volunteer was me. I saw firsthand how much the scoreboard depended on one person’s attention: a forgotten out, a miscounted run, or an out-of-sync slide could break the experience for the whole crowd in seconds. That friction, repeated tournament after tournament, became a design problem I wanted to solve.
case.baseball.users.card1.title: Operator
case.baseball.users.card1.body: Logs every play in real time while watching the game.
case.baseball.users.card1.need: Needs: speed and zero errors without looking away from the field.
case.baseball.users.card2.title: Coordinator
case.baseball.users.card2.body: Registers teams and the batting order before each game.
case.baseball.users.card2.need: Needs: to set up the game without interfering with live scoring.
case.baseball.users.card3.title: Projection team
case.baseball.users.card3.body: Runs the screen the audience sees, without touching game scoring.
case.baseball.users.card3.need: Needs: a screen that stays in sync on its own.
case.baseball.users.card4.title: Audience
case.baseball.users.card4.body: Follows the score on the big screen, from a distance.
case.baseball.users.card4.need: Needs: to understand the state of the game at a glance.
case.baseball.constraint1: No reliable internet at the field: the system had to work fully offline.
case.baseball.constraint2: A live game doesn’t pause for corrections: every fix happens while play continues.
case.baseball.constraint3: Volunteers with little time to learn a new tool.
case.baseball.constraint4: Bible Baseball has its own rules, and they weren’t written down anywhere.
case.baseball.context.hard: What made it hard: the operator has to watch the field and the interface at the same time, and everything they do shows up instantly on a public screen.
case.baseball.problem.heading: The missing piece wasn’t a scoreboard. It was a safe way to run one.
case.baseball.problem.statement: How can one person score a live game without visible mistakes when their attention is split between the field and the screen?
case.baseball.problem.body: To answer that, the solution had to:
case.baseball.problem.goal1: Make scoring mistakes hard to make and easy to fix.
case.baseball.problem.goal3: Work completely without an internet connection.
case.baseball.problem.goal4: Build in the specific rules of Bible Baseball.
case.baseball.research.heading: Understanding the domain before designing a single screen
case.baseball.research.m1.body: I ran the scoreboard as a volunteer in previous editions of the tournament, using whiteboards and PowerPoint.
case.baseball.research.m2.body: I watched several tournaments to understand the real pace of a game and the moments when pressure builds up.
case.baseball.research.m3.body: I documented the rules of Bible Baseball, which had never been written down, and checked everything I didn’t know with the organizers.
case.baseball.research.m4.body: I started from the PowerPoint in use to identify which information was essential to keep and what could go.
case.baseball.research.errorsHead: The mistakes the tool had to prevent
case.baseball.research.goal2: Recording the wrong number of runs
case.evidence.label: About the evidence:
case.baseball.research.evidence: The research was qualitative and informal: it’s based on my direct experience as the operator, observing games, and conversations with the organizers. There were no structured interviews or formal usability tests with other operators.
case.baseball.insights.heading: Three insights that shaped the design
case.baseball.insight1.title: Most actions repeat dozens of times per game.
case.baseball.insight1.body: Out, run, change of inning. Frequency — not the structure of the sport — had to organize the interface.
case.baseball.insight2.title: Mistakes came from split attention, not from not knowing the rules.
case.baseball.insight2.body: The operator knows the game, but watches the field and the screen at once. Mistakes were going to happen; the design had to make them hard to make and cheap to fix.
case.baseball.insight3.title: The operator and the audience need different information.
case.baseball.insight3.body: The operator needs controls and detail; the audience needs to read the state of the game from a distance. One view for both serves neither.
case.baseball.decisions.heading: Every decision answers an observed problem
case.baseball.d1.title: One click for frequent actions
case.baseball.d1.problem: Recording an out or a run meant editing and recalculating by hand while the game went on.
case.baseball.d1.insight: The most frequent actions repeat dozens of times per game.
case.baseball.d1.decision: Each frequent action is an always-visible button; rarely used settings stay hidden until needed.
case.baseball.d1.why: Fewer steps and less cognitive load while attention is on the field, not the screen.
case.baseball.d2.title: A projection designed on its own, not a mirror of the console
case.baseball.d2.problem: Projecting the console would expose controls, internal data, and in-between states to the audience.
case.baseball.d2.insight: The audience needs to read the score from a distance; the operator needs controls.
case.baseball.d2.decision: A dedicated projection view, synced with the console, showing only the essential score at a large size.
case.baseball.d2.why: Legible from a distance, with no controls exposed on the public screen.
case.baseball.d3.title: Prevent and recover instead of demanding perfection
case.baseball.d3.problem: One wrong tap mid-game could wipe out information with no way back.
case.baseball.d3.insight: With split attention, mistakes will happen.
case.baseball.d3.decision: Separate destructive actions from frequent ones, ask for confirmation on anything irreversible, and log every play in a history that supports undo.
case.baseball.d3.why: Fix mistakes without stopping the game or recalculating the score by hand.
case.baseball.d3.tradeoff: undo only covers the last play; older corrections are made from the play history. Keeping it to one level makes it predictable under pressure.
case.baseball.d4.title: Work without internet, without a server
case.baseball.d4.problem: The field has no reliable connection, and the audience screen had to update on its own.
case.baseball.d4.insight: Relying on a server would turn any network failure into a frozen scoreboard in front of everyone.
case.baseball.d4.decision: Sync the console and the projection inside the browser, on the same computer, with no server.
case.baseball.d4.why: The system behaves the same with or without a network, with fewer parts that can fail live.
case.baseball.d4.tradeoff: both views must run on the same machine. An optional backend was added later to sync multiple devices, without removing local mode.
case.minor.head: Smaller decisions
case.baseball.minor1.title: Dark mode
case.baseball.minor1.body: Meant to reduce the operator’s eye strain over days with several back-to-back games. It’s a design intent, not something I measured.
case.baseball.minor2.title: Rules built in
case.baseball.minor2.body: The rules of Bible Baseball live in the system, not in the operator’s memory.
case.baseball.minor3.title: Minimum information
case.baseball.minor3.body: Each screen shows only what the task at hand requires.
case.baseball.minor4.title: Learnable in minutes
case.baseball.minor4.body: Designed for volunteers who have no time for training before the tournament.
case.baseball.iteration.heading: From whiteboard to console, validated on the field
case.baseball.before1: Physical whiteboards and PowerPoint slides updated by hand.
case.baseball.before2: The operator recalculates the score in their head.
case.baseball.before3: The audience screen knows nothing about the game: it has to be edited separately.
case.baseball.before.diagram: Diagram: the operator writes on the whiteboard and also edits by hand the slide sent to the projector — two separate tasks.
case.baseball.explore1: Sketches on top of the existing PowerPoint to decide which information to keep.
case.baseball.explore2: A working prototype in Figma Make to validate the layout and the operating flow.
case.baseball.explore3: AI-assisted exploration of interface alternatives and edge cases.
case.baseball.explore4: Running it as the operator in real games: new rules surfaced and were added between editions.
case.baseball.discarded: a single view for both operator and audience. It showed controls to the crowd and hid information from the operator.
case.baseball.after1: One click for frequent actions, always visible.
case.baseball.after2: The projection updates itself from the console.
case.baseball.after3: Works offline, with the rules built in.
case.baseball.after.diagram: Diagram: the operator logs a play once in the console and the projection updates automatically.
case.baseball.ai.body: I used AI to explore interface alternatives, review flows, and catch edge cases before prototyping, and as a coding copilot during implementation. I reviewed, adapted, and tested every change; the product, experience, and interface decisions were mine and were validated in real use.
case.baseball.product.heading: What ran at the tournament
case.baseball.img.console: Operator console: play logging, count, runners on base, and runs per inning
case.baseball.cap1.title: Operator console · D1, D3
case.baseball.cap1.body: Frequent actions are always in view; bases, count, and runs per inning can be read at a glance. Destructive actions are kept apart from frequent ones.
case.baseball.img.projection: Projection screen: score, team at bat, bases, and runs per inning
case.baseball.cap2.title: Projection screen · D2
case.baseball.cap2.body: Only what the audience needs: score, team at bat, bases, and runs per inning, legible from a distance. No controls visible.
case.baseball.img.history: Play history by inning, team, player, and time
case.baseball.cap3.title: Play history · D3
case.baseball.cap3.body: Every play is logged by inning, team, player, and time — the basis for fixing mistakes without recalculating.
case.baseball.cap4.title: Dark mode
case.baseball.cap4.body: The same console, for long days with several back-to-back games.
case.baseball.results.heading: What I know, what I didn’t measure, and what I expected
case.results.measuredKind: What I can claim with evidence.
case.baseball.results.measured1: The system was used throughout the tournament.
case.baseball.results.measured2: Real use surfaced rules that hadn’t been accounted for; they were added in later iterations.
case.baseball.results.measured3: I didn’t measure error rates or timings before and after, so I don’t report quantitative improvements.
case.baseball.results.expected1: Fewer scoring mistakes visible to the audience.
case.baseball.results.expected2: Lower cognitive load for the operator.
case.baseball.results.expected3: A public screen that’s always in sync.
case.baseball.results.note: The system is planned to be used again in future editions of the tournament.
case.baseball.learnings.heading: What I’m taking with me — and what I’d change
case.baseball.learn1.title: Domain first
case.baseball.learn1.body: The rules and the real pace of a game weren’t written down anywhere. Without that fieldwork, any interface would have solved the wrong problem.
case.baseball.learn2.title: Design against real pressure
case.baseball.learn2.body: An operator in the middle of a game has no time to think about the interface. Every decision had to be judged against that pressure, not against an ideal scenario.
case.baseball.learn3.title: Measure a baseline before replacing the process
case.baseball.learn3.body: Logging how many mistakes and corrections happened with whiteboards and PowerPoint would have let me talk about impact with data, not just with how it felt to use.
case.baseball.learn4.title: Validation comes mostly from my own use
case.baseball.learn4.body: I was the main operator. With more time, I’d test the system with volunteers who haven’t seen it before, to check whether it really can be learned in minutes.
case.baseball.tech.heading: The technical decisions that shaped the experience
case.baseball.tech.intro: Designing and building the product myself let me treat technical constraints as part of the design, not something discovered at the end.
case.baseball.tech1.title: Local sync, no server
case.baseball.tech1.body: The console and the projection communicate through localStorage and StorageEvent within the same browser.
case.baseball.tech1.impact: In the experience: the public screen updates itself even without a network (D4).
case.baseball.tech2.title: Rules as pure functions
case.baseball.tech2.body: Game logic (outs, runs, innings, special rules) lives apart from the interface and has unit tests.
case.baseball.tech2.impact: In the experience: every new rule found on the field can be adjusted without breaking the interface.
case.baseball.tech3.title: History and undo
case.baseball.tech3.body: Every play is logged with its context, and a snapshot of the game state is saved before it’s applied.
case.baseball.tech3.impact: In the experience: undo and correct without recalculating by hand (D3).
case.baseball.tech4.title: Growing without losing local mode
case.baseball.tech4.body: There’s now also an optional backend (Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL) to sync multiple devices and manage roles.
case.baseball.tech4.impact: In the experience: offline mode is still the default.

meta.kerygma.title: Kerygma Stage — Case study | Gregory Durán
case.kerygma.hero.subtitle: Presentation software for live church services, built around one idea: what the operator prepares and what the congregation sees should never be the same thing until the operator decides it is.
case.kerygma.hero.imageAlt: Operator console with separate preview and live views, next to the remote control on a phone
case.kerygma.overview.heading: The project in 30 seconds
case.kerygma.ov.product: Desktop software for projecting lyrics, Bible verses, and announcements during a live service.
case.kerygma.ov.context: Volunteer teams at churches using PowerPoint, Google Slides, or tools like ProPresenter. Used weekly by Iglesia Hogar de Salvación y Alabanza.
case.kerygma.ov.problem: In general-purpose tools, preparing means exposing: fixing a typo, finding a verse, or improvising all happens in front of the entire congregation.
case.kerygma.ov.role: Product Designer and full-stack developer, end to end: research, architecture, interaction and UI design, front end (React), and native back end (Rust).
case.kerygma.ov.platform: Desktop (Windows) + remote control from a phone
case.kerygma.context.heading: A live service can’t be redone
case.kerygma.context.p1: Many churches project lyrics and verses with PowerPoint or Google Slides, which were built for office presentations, or with tools like ProPresenter, whose cost and complexity don’t always fit a volunteer team.
case.kerygma.context.p2: Kerygma Stage was built for that context: a volunteer working under pressure, with no guaranteed internet, in front of a congregation that should never see a mistake.
case.kerygma.context.usersHead: Three audiences at the same moment
case.kerygma.users.card1.title: Operator
case.kerygma.users.card1.body: Picks and projects lyrics, verses, and announcements in real time.
case.kerygma.users.card1.need: Needs: to see and prepare what’s next before the audience sees it.
case.kerygma.users.card2.title: Preacher and musicians
case.kerygma.users.card2.body: Follow the service from the stage.
case.kerygma.users.card2.need: Need: their own screen with the current text, what’s next, a clock, and chords — without turning toward the audience screen.
case.kerygma.users.card3.title: Congregation
case.kerygma.users.card3.need: Needs: legible text and no half-finished changes.
case.kerygma.constraint1: Church Wi-Fi isn’t reliable: the service can’t depend on the internet.
case.kerygma.constraint2: Service audio is sensitive: it shouldn’t leave the building.
case.kerygma.constraint3: Volunteer operators with very different levels of experience.
case.kerygma.constraint4: An unpredictable pace: a verse quoted without warning has to appear within seconds.
case.kerygma.problem.heading: General-purpose tools for a job that isn’t
case.kerygma.problem.statement: With a single shared view, everything the operator does — preparing, fixing, searching — happens in front of the congregation.
case.kerygma.problem.body: The problems operators report again and again:
case.kerygma.problem.goal1: You can’t see what’s coming without the audience already seeing it.
case.kerygma.problem.goal2: Fixing a mistake live exposes the mistake while it’s being fixed.
case.kerygma.problem.goal3: Inserting an unplanned verse or quote is slow.
case.kerygma.problem.goal4: Line breaks split long lyrics and verses in awkward places.
case.kerygma.problem.goal5: The preacher has no useful confidence monitor.
case.kerygma.research.heading: Reported problems, not assumptions
case.kerygma.research.m1.body: I compiled the ten problems most often reported by operators of PowerPoint, Google Slides, and ProPresenter, and the ten features they ask for most.
case.kerygma.research.m2.body: I compared how those tools handle (or don’t) previewing, live editing, and finding content.
case.kerygma.research.m3.body: Services at my own church provided a real context for understanding the pace of a service and setting priorities.
case.kerygma.research.m4.body: Every feature is tested in a real service — with a real microphone, phone, and monitors — before it’s considered done.
case.kerygma.research.priority: I prioritized by reported impact, not by what was most technically interesting to build.
case.kerygma.research.evidence: The initial research is secondary (problems reported by operators) and doesn’t include formal interviews. Validation comes from weekly use at one church and from testing in real services.
case.kerygma.insights.heading: Three insights that shaped the product
case.kerygma.insight1.title: The core problem wasn’t features — it was visibility.
case.kerygma.insight1.body: Most of the reported problems come from the same root: one view shared by the operator and the audience.
case.kerygma.insight2.title: An automatic mistake in front of the congregation costs more than a slow manual action.
case.kerygma.insight2.body: Automation helps find content quickly, but the operator is the one accountable in front of the audience.
case.kerygma.insight3.title: Connectivity and privacy decide whether the product works on any given Sunday.
case.kerygma.insight3.body: They’re not technical details: if something depends on the internet or sends audio out, it doesn’t work in this context.
case.kerygma.decisions.heading: Three decisions that matter more than every feature combined
case.kerygma.d1.title: Preview vs. live
case.kerygma.d1.problem: Preparing the next slide or fixing a mistake happened in front of everyone.
case.kerygma.d1.insight: The operator and the congregation need to see different things at the same moment.
case.kerygma.d1.decision: Two separate areas: the operator prepares and reviews in the preview; nothing reaches the projection until they confirm it — even when editing live.
case.kerygma.d1.why: The audience never sees a half-finished change, and the operator can work ahead without fear.
case.kerygma.d1.tradeoff: every change takes one extra step (confirming). Keyboard shortcuts for frequent actions offset that cost.
case.kerygma.img.console: Operator console: the next slide in preview while another one is live
case.kerygma.d1.cap: The next slide waits in the preview while another one is live.
case.kerygma.d2.title: Suggest vs. automate
case.kerygma.d2.problem: Verses are quoted during the sermon without warning, and looking them up by hand is slow.
case.kerygma.d2.insight: Voice detection can get confused (for example, “John” vs. “1 John”), and a wrong change in front of the congregation is worse than a slow one.
case.kerygma.d2.decision: When the system detects a Bible reference in what’s being said, it suggests it to the operator in a notice. The projection doesn’t change until the operator confirms.
case.kerygma.d2.why: AI saves the search; judgment — and accountability in front of the audience — stays with the operator.
case.kerygma.d2.discarded: letting detection change the projection on its own. It would have been faster, but an automatic mistake in front of the whole congregation can’t be quietly undone.
case.kerygma.d3.title: Offline-first
case.kerygma.d3.problem: Wi-Fi isn’t reliable, and transcribing in the cloud would mean sending everything said in the service outside the building.
case.kerygma.d3.insight: Connectivity and privacy decide whether the product can be used in this context at all.
case.kerygma.d3.decision: Everything works with no connection and no account. Captions and verse detection run on the device; the remote control uses the local network, not the internet.
case.kerygma.d3.why: The service doesn’t depend on the network, and the audio never leaves the device.
case.kerygma.d3.tradeoff: local transcription depends on the computer’s hardware and takes more engineering work (models, performance, microphone permissions) than a cloud API.
case.kerygma.img.remote: Remote control on a phone: previous, next, and blackout
case.kerygma.d3.cap: The remote control works from a phone over the local network, with no internet.
case.kerygma.iteration.heading: From a shared PowerPoint to two separate views
case.kerygma.before1: A single view: whatever the operator touches is what the audience sees.
case.kerygma.before2: Fixing a mistake live means everyone watches it being fixed.
case.kerygma.before3: Inserting an unplanned verse means leaving the presentation and searching by hand.
case.kerygma.explore1: Prioritizing based on problems reported by operators.
case.kerygma.explore2: Separating preview and live as the structural change.
case.kerygma.explore3: Redesigning the architecture as local-first, with its own data model.
case.kerygma.explore4: Visual redesign: Inter typography, flat surfaces, and a single accent color, designed for hours of use under pressure.
case.kerygma.explore5: Testing in real services with a real microphone, phone, and monitors.
case.kerygma.discarded: cloud transcription, and verse detection that changes the projection on its own.
case.kerygma.after2: Live editing without exposing half-finished changes.
case.kerygma.after3: The Bible and song library one shortcut (Ctrl+K) away.
case.kerygma.img.grid: Console in grid mode with every slide of the service grouped by section
case.kerygma.iteration.findingsHead: What only showed up with real hardware
case.kerygma.finding2: A real-time audio algorithm that caused dropouts.
case.kerygma.finding3: Inconsistent transcription of spoken numbers — critical for chapters and verses.
case.kerygma.iteration.findingsNote: No unit test caught these problems; testing in a real service did.
case.kerygma.ai.body: I used AI as a coding copilot during implementation, reviewing, adapting, and testing the generated code in real services. The research, prioritization, and product and design decisions were mine.

case.kerygma.f.library.body: Songs with tags, key, and BPM so they’re quick to find.
case.kerygma.f.captions.title: Live captions
case.kerygma.f.captions.body: Real-time speech transcription, processed on the device.
case.kerygma.f.verses.title: Verse detection
case.kerygma.f.verses.body: Recognizes Bible references in what’s being said and suggests them to the operator (D2).
case.kerygma.results.heading: Real use, no inflated metrics
case.kerygma.results.stat1: use in services at Iglesia Hogar de Salvación y Alabanza
case.kerygma.results.stat2: audiences served by the same app: operator, stage, and congregation
case.kerygma.results.measured1: Testing in real services surfaced problems the tests didn’t catch (microphone, audio, spoken numbers), and they were fixed.
case.kerygma.results.measured2: There are no formal metrics yet — such as on-screen mistakes or time to insert a verse — comparing before and after.
case.kerygma.results.expected1: The congregation doesn’t see mistakes or half-finished changes.
case.kerygma.results.expected3: The service doesn’t depend on connectivity.
case.kerygma.learnings.heading: What I’m taking with me — and what I’d change
case.kerygma.learn1.title: Designing for two audiences at once
case.kerygma.learn1.body: The operator and the congregation need to see different things at the same moment. That tension — not aesthetics — was the central design problem.
case.kerygma.learn2.title: Offline is a product decision
case.kerygma.learn2.body: Processing everything locally turned out to be a product advantage (reliability and privacy), not just a technical constraint.
case.kerygma.learn3.title: Define how to measure from the start
case.kerygma.learn3.body: Tracking, for example, how many live corrections happen or how long it takes to insert a verse would let me talk about impact with data.
case.kerygma.learn4.title: A single validation context
case.kerygma.learn4.body: It’s validated mainly at one church. With more time, I’d test it with operators from other churches and with new volunteers.
case.kerygma.tech.heading: Architecture in service of the design decisions
case.kerygma.tech1.title: One renderer for every screen
case.kerygma.tech1.body: The preview, the confidence monitor, and the projection share the same component, on a fixed 1280×720 logical canvas that scales to each monitor.
case.kerygma.tech1.impact: In the experience: what the operator reviews is exactly what the audience will see (D1).
case.kerygma.tech2.title: On-device transcription
case.kerygma.tech2.body: whisper.cpp, integrated in Rust, captures the microphone and transcribes locally.
case.kerygma.tech2.impact: In the experience: captions and verse suggestions with no internet and no cloud (D2, D3).
case.kerygma.tech3.title: A server on the local network
case.kerygma.tech3.body: An HTTP and WebSocket server (Axum) inside the app serves a simple page to the operator’s phone.
case.kerygma.tech3.impact: In the experience: remote control without depending on the internet (D3).
case.kerygma.tech4.title: Native desktop with Tauri
case.kerygma.tech4.body: A React interface on a Rust back end, with access to the microphone, network, files, and monitors without bundling a full browser.
case.kerygma.tech4.impact: In the experience: multi-monitor support and global shortcuts a web app couldn’t offer.
meta.nexo.title: Nexo — Concept project | Gregory Durán
case.nexo.hero.subtitle: An exploration of a mobile app that brings essential public services together: checking, paying, reporting issues, and tracking them in one place.
case.nexo.status.label: Status:
case.nexo.status.body: This is a concept, not a shipped product. It has no users and no measured results; what follows describes the problem and the design direction I’m exploring.
case.nexo.problem.heading: Scattered services, requests with no follow-up
case.nexo.problem.body: Each public service (water, electricity, and others) lives in its own channel: different apps, offices, and processes. Citizens have no single place to check, pay, or follow up on a report, and once they report an outage they lose sight of its status.
case.nexo.direction.heading: Hypotheses I’m exploring
case.nexo.decisions.card1.title: The service card as the core unit
case.nexo.decisions.card1.body: Each service with a visible status (up to date, pending, issue reported) so the whole dashboard can be scanned at a glance.
case.nexo.decisions.card2.title: A single reporting flow
case.nexo.decisions.card2.body: One flow with conditional fields depending on the service, instead of a different form for each one.
case.nexo.decisions.card3.title: Status always visible
case.nexo.decisions.card3.body: Every payment or report tied to a status (received, in progress, resolved) visible from the main dashboard.
case.nexo.decisions.card4.title: Still to be validated
case.nexo.decisions.card4.body: These hypotheses still need research with citizens before they become decisions.
case.nexo.cta.title: In the meantime, see work in real use
